sentences.text: Tralkasaurus is a genus of abelisaurid dinosaur found in the Huincul Formation of Río Negro Province, Argentina.
It is a medium-sized member of this group that mixes traits from early-diverging forms with those of the specialized Brachyrostra clade, making its exact classification uncertain.
The maxilla, a subtriangular bone on the upper jaw, measures 22 centimeters in length, which is smaller than the 32-centimeter maxilla of the similarly sized dinosaur Skorpiovenator.
This bone is covered in neurovascular foramina and rugosities.
The maxilla contained eleven tooth sockets, four of which held preserved teeth.
Unlike Skorpiovenator, the serrations on both edges of these teeth were the same size, a feature similar to that seen in Majungasaurus.
Tralkasaurus is unique among abelisaurids for having the front margin of its antorbital fenestra slope forwards and upwards.
Additionally, forward and backward projecting processes on its tail vertebrae overlapped, a trait characteristic of the Brachyrostra clade.
The animal also shared key abelisaurid traits including a deep maxilla, fused interdental plates, specific vertebral connections, inclined tail processes, and a thin pubic shaft.
The pubis itself measures 35 centimeters in length.
The name Tralkasaurus cuyi translates to 'thunder lizard of El Cuy,' referencing the Mapudungun word for thunder and the discovery village.
Despite its unique skull features, the complete animal measured only 6 meters in length.
The fossil site known as Rancho Violante, located near the village of El Cuy in Río Negro province, was discovered in 1999 by Sebastián Apesteguía.
Tralkasaurus was formally described in 2020 by Mauricio Cerroni and colleagues.
The holotype specimen, catalogued as MPCA-Pv 815, consists of an incomplete skeleton including a maxilla, various vertebrae, ribs, and a poorly preserved pubis.
Tralkasaurus coexisted with titanosaurian sauropods and an ornithopod in the Huincul Formation ecosystem.
Numerous theropods are known from Rancho Violante, including Gualicho, Aoniraptor, Taurovenator, an unenlagine, and an unnamed carcarodontosaurid.
Phylogenetic analysis places Tralkasaurus among basal abelisaurids but fails to resolve its exact relationship to other species due to conflicting traits.
Tralkasaurus lived in what is now South America, specifically in the Huincul Formation of Argentina.
The fossils belong to the Cenomanian-Turonian age of the Huincul Formation, yet the animal is also stated to have lived during the Albian stage, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago.

Tralkasaurus exhibits a conflicting combination of features, with caudal transverse process projections typical of Brachyrostra but extensive antorbital fossae that are plesiomorphic like basal abelsauroids.
Phylogenetic analysis placed Tralkasaurus as a basal abelisaurid but could not resolve its affinities beyond a polytomy.
